dataset_family: US Health and Retirement Study (HRS), 1998 baseline sub-cohort followed to 2018 (Waves 4-14); nationally representative US adults aged 50+; analytic N 9,317 (depression to MCI) and 9,428 (MCI to depression)
method_family: Population-based longitudinal survey cohort: competing-risks (sub-distribution hazard) regression of incident psychometrically defined MCI on baseline binary high-risk depressive symptoms (CES-D-8 >= 4), and the reverse direction, with gender and education interaction terms; multilevel growth-curve sensitivity models with continuous CES-D and composite cognitive scores
what_it_shows: In HRS over 20 years, baseline high-risk depressive symptoms (CES-D-8 >= 4) predicted incident MCI in competing-risks models (SHR 1.38 unadjusted; 1.20, 1.08-1.34, fully adjusted; N = 9,317), and baseline MCI predicted incident high-risk depressive symptoms (fully adjusted SHR 1.16, 1.01-1.33; N = 9,428). Neither gender nor education moderated either direction. People with MCI or dementia (or with high-risk depressive symptoms) at baseline were excluded, so there is no analysis of MCI prognosis or MCI neurobiology. A sensitivity analysis with continuous CES-D is reported in words only (Supplement V, not in the extract): higher baseline CES-D predicted steeper cognitive decline.
why: Guo, Pai, Xue and Lu, J Affect Disord 338 (2023) 449-458, DOI 10.1016/j.jad.2023.06.046. The PDF title, authors and DOI match the summaries.md block and the map entry. Against the Table A1 statement, the study supports the FIRST clause (depression status is associated with MCI) with its own analysis: a binary screen-positive depressive-symptom status predicts incident MCI, and MCI predicts incident depressive symptoms, over 20 years. Round 20 found that neither P-643 nor P-647 tests this clause. The study does NOT bear on the row's substantive claim about severity: all participants were free of MCI at baseline, there are no brain measures, and there is no MCI-to-dementia outcome. MCI is a composite-score band (7-11 of 27) from the HRS interview battery, not a clinical diagnosis, and 'subsequent MCI' includes people who reached the dementia band. The paper's only continuous-severity analysis (growth curves) found higher CES-D associated with steeper cognitive decline in people without MCI. If it points anywhere, that result points toward severity grading cognitive course (the P-26 side of the row). But it is in a non-MCI population, it concerns a cognitive score rather than conversion, and its coefficients are in a supplement that is not available here, so it is recorded as context, not as counter-evidence. 'Status' here is a CES-D-8 >= 4 screen, not a clinical diagnosis of depression. Limits the authors name: a limited composite cognitive measure; selection bias from missing data (excluded participants more often had the baseline exposures); residual confounding. Verdict 'partly', for the first clause only, on the same standard round 1 applied to P-720 and P-785. Independence: HRS is not the dataset of any current supporter (Korea University Guro; Shanghai Brain Health Cohort; Shanghai Tongji; Florence) or of any round-1 or round-2 candidate (P-785 is HCHS/SOL, P-954 is WHICAP), and no authors are shared. Not a preprint. Quotes are transliterated to ASCII (>= for the greater-or-equal sign, - for en dashes).

quotes.quote: After full adjustment, baseline high-risk depressive symptoms were significantly associated with subsequent MCI (SHR = 1.20, 95%CI 1.08-1.34). Participants with baseline MCI are more likely to develop subsequent high-risk depressive symptoms than those without baseline MCI (SHR = 1.16, 95%CI 1.01-1.33).
We further excluded samples who already reported outcome of interest (MCI/dementia; high-risk depressive symptoms) at baseline

A modified version of the Centre for Epidemiological Studies-Depression (CES-D) scale (8-item scale; yes/no; 0-8) was used to measure depressive symptoms. Higher scores reflect higher level of depressive symptoms. High-risk depressive symptoms are indicated when the total score is >=4 (Mojtabai and Olfson, 2004).

When the total scores were between 0-6, 7-11 and 12-27, participants were considered to have dementia, MCI without dementia, and normal respectively (Crimmins et al., 2011). We used binary variables for MCI as the outcome (1 = subsequent MCI [including cases with subsequent dementia, assuming subsequent MCI occurred in the midterm between baseline and dementia occurrence]; 0 = normal)

First, as the results in Supplements V and VI show, in unadjusted, minimally adjusted, and fully adjusted models, participants with higher CES-D scores at baseline were more likely to have decreased trajectories of cognitive functioning at subsequent follow-up

Second, selection bias may exist due to attrition and non-responsiveness. According to results in Supplement IV, those in excluded sample were more likely to have baseline exposure, but less likely to have higher education
We re-run all statistical models using continuous CES-D and composite cognitive scores. Results were consistent with the original results based on dichotomous variables.
